readerTitle: Enron: the most innovative company nobody could explain
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Enron, Arthur Andersen) + 가상 적용 (생활용품 소매 체인과 도매업체)
insight: 사업이 어떻게 현금을 버는지 쉬운 말로 설명할 수 없다면, 그 복잡함 자체가 경고 신호다. 경고 신호 하나는 해명될 수 있지만 여러 개가 겹치면 판단을 멈추고 질문해야 한다.
misconception: 유명 감사법인이 승인하고 언론이 칭찬하는 회사라면 숫자를 믿어도 된다. 이해하기 어려운 재무제표는 그만큼 정교한 사업이라는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Powers, W. C. et al. (2002). Report of Investigation by the Special Investigative Committee of the Board of Directors of Enron Corp. (Powers Report): 파트너십, CFO 이해충돌, 윤리규정 면제, 재무제표 재작성
McLean, B. (2001, March 5). Is Enron Overpriced? Fortune: Enron이 어떻게 돈을 버는지 설명하기 어렵다는 지적
US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (2002). The Role of the Financial Institutions in Enron's Collapse: 은행 선불 거래(prepay)가 사실상 대출이었다는 분석
Enron Corp. 2000 Annual Report / Form 10-K: 2000년 매출 약 $101B, 1999년 약 $40B
Enron Corp. Form 8-K (2001년 11월 8일): 1997년 이후 실적 재작성. 2001년 10월 16일 3분기 실적 발표: 손실 및 자기자본 $1.2B 감소
Arthur Andersen LLP v. United States, 544 U.S. 696 (2005): 2002년 유죄 판결 파기. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002

factChecks.note: Fortune의 'America's Most Innovative Company' 6년 연속(1996~2001년 선정) 선정 여부를 Fortune 원자료로 확인하세요.
2000년 매출 약 $101B(1999년 약 $40B, 즉 두 배 이상 증가)를 2000년 10-K로 확인하세요. 매출을 거래 총액 기준(gross)으로 잡은 점은 당시 회계 규칙 해석 문제로 널리 비판받았습니다. 카드에는 불법이라고 단정하지 않았습니다.
주가 고점 약 $90(2000년 8월), 2001년 11월 말 $1 미만 하락을 주가 자료로 확인하세요.
Skilling은 2001년 2월 CEO가 되었고 8월에 사임했습니다(약 6개월). 2001년 10월 16일 손실 발표와 자기자본 $1.2B 감소, 11월 재작성(1997년까지 소급), 12월 2일 파산 신청(당시 미국 최대 규모, 2002년 WorldCom이 넘어섬)을 다시 확인하세요.
Blockbuster와의 VOD 합작에서 시범 단계를 넘지 못했는데도 큰 이익을 미리 잡았다는 내용은 WSJ 보도와 Powers Report에 나옵니다. 정확한 금액은 출처마다 달라 카드에는 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 이미지와 문장에 회사명이나 로고를 쓰지 않았습니다.
Andersen이 감사 보수 외에 큰 컨설팅 보수를 받았다는 점은 널리 보도되었습니다. 정확한 금액은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 2002년 사법방해 유죄, 2005년 대법원 파기를 확인하세요.
이사회가 Fastow의 LJM 파트너십 운영을 위해 윤리규정을 면제한 사실은 Powers Report에 나옵니다.

cards.title: Enron: the most innovative company nobody could explain
body: Fortune magazine named Enron America's most innovative company six years in a row. In 2000, the Houston energy trader reported about $100 billion in revenue, more than double the year before.
In December 2001, it filed for bankruptcy. The warning signs had been in plain view for months.

image.label: A gleaming office tower with cracks running through its base
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반짝이는 고층 빌딩, 꼭대기에는 트로피와 상승 그래프. 아래쪽 기초에는 가는 금이 여러 갈래로 퍼져 있음. 실제 회사 로고, 'E' 상징, 회사명은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's early 2001. Do you invest?
body: You're deciding whether to put serious money into Enron. Revenue has doubled. Profits are rising. A big-name auditor has signed off.
But a Fortune reporter writes that even experts can't explain how Enron makes its money. The footnotes mention deals with partnerships run by its own finance chief.

options.text: Invest. The growth is real and the auditor approved the books
options.feedback: You get the upside of a market favorite. But you're trusting other people's checks without doing your own.

options.text: Hold off until you can explain how profit turns into cash
options.feedback: You might miss some gains. But if a company's money trail can't be followed, you can't judge the risk you're taking.

options.text: Invest a smaller amount and watch the next few quarters
options.feedback: Smaller bets limit the damage. But it's still a bet on numbers you don't understand, and the news can turn faster than you can react.

cards.title: From market darling to bankruptcy in 16 months.
body: Employees who held Enron shares in their retirement accounts saw much of their savings disappear.

breakdown.label: CEO quits
breakdown.detail: Jeff Skilling leaves after about six months in the job

breakdown.label: First crack
breakdown.detail: A quarterly loss and a $1.2 billion cut to shareholders' equity

breakdown.label: Bankruptcy
breakdown.detail: The largest in US history at the time

cards.title: Complexity is a red flag
body: **Complexity as a red flag** means this: if you can't explain in plain words how a business turns sales into cash, treat the confusion as a warning, not as a sign of genius.
At Enron, complexity was where the problems hid. Each odd deal had an explanation. The explanations just never added up to a simple story of money coming in.

image.label: A tangled knot of arrows between boxes, with cash missing at the end
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 'Sales'에서 출발한 화살표가 여러 상자('Partnership', 'Trade', 'Estimate')를 복잡하게 돌다가 'Cash' 상자에 도착하지 못하고 끊김. 옆에는 단순한 화살표 하나로 Sales→Cash가 이어진 비교 그림.

cards.softwareNote: Software companies face the same test with multi-year contracts, "bookings" and adjusted metrics. If the path from a signed deal to cash in the bank needs a long explanation, ask for it.

cards.title: Four red flags, stacked together.
body: Each of these appeared in the unit's earlier lessons. Enron had all of them at once.
list: **Profit booked on day one:** under *mark-to-market* accounting, Enron recorded its own estimate of a long deal's future profit when it was signed. One video venture never got past a pilot.
**Borrowed cash dressed as earned cash:** some bank deals worked like loans but were recorded as trades.
**Debt parked off the books:** partnerships, some run by finance chief Andrew Fastow, took on debt and troubled assets.
**Revenue counted in full:** many trades were booked at their whole value, not just Enron's cut.
cards.callout: One flag can be explained away. Four together describe a company no outsider could check.

cards.title: The watchers had reasons not to look.
body: Arthur Andersen, Enron's auditor, also earned large consulting fees from it. When a professional firm is paid well to advise the client it audits, saying no gets expensive.

Enron's board waived its own ethics code so the finance chief could run partnerships that traded with Enron. After the collapse, Andersen staff destroyed Enron documents. The firm's 2002 conviction was later overturned, but it collapsed anyway. Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in 2002 to tighten oversight.

image.label: An inspector holding a magnifying glass while being handed a bag of money
image.brief: 일러스트. 정장 차림 검사관이 돋보기를 들고 있지만 시선은 옆에서 건네받는 돈 봉투를 향함. 실제 회사명이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Complex doesn't mean crooked.
body: Banks, insurers and global manufacturers are complex for honest reasons. Hindsight also makes Enron's flags look brighter than they did in 2001, when many smart investors stayed in.

Use complexity as a reason to ask questions, not as proof of fraud. The real warning is when the questions get vague answers, or when asking them gets you treated as someone who just doesn't understand.

cards.title: Now you're a wholesaler.
body: A fast-growing chain of home-goods stores wants you as its exclusive supplier. It will pay in 120 days instead of your usual 30.
Its reported profits are soaring. But its cash balance keeps falling, and its stores are leased from a company owned by the founder. What do you do?

options.text: Sign. Profits like that mean they can pay
options.feedback: You win a big customer fast. But profit that never shows up as cash may never show up as your payment either.

options.text: Ask them to walk you through where the cash goes, and start on short terms
options.feedback: You may lose the deal if they refuse. If they explain clearly, you've gained a customer you understand.

options.text: Sign, but cap how much they can owe you at any time
options.feedback: A credit cap limits your loss. It doesn't tell you whether the business behind the order is sound.

cards.title: If you can't trace profit to cash, don't trust the profit.
body: Enron's flags were visible. What failed was the willingness to keep asking until the story made sense.
**Try it today:** pick your biggest customer or supplier. In three sentences, explain how they turn sales into cash. Where you get stuck is where to ask.
